extracted.intended_audience: general readers of essays and reflective philosophy; people interested in practical moral counsel
extracted.subtask_description: A reflective personal essay (Montaigne) giving normative guidance about judgment, friendship, conversation, solitude, reading, ageing, and conduct. The text offers practical maxims and examples rather than formalized rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advise candidly and clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: When friends ask for advice, give it candidly and clearly without sticking, even at the hazard of the thing’s falling out contrary to your opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not refuse the office of advising because your counsel may be reproached later; the fault will be theirs for consulting you if they choose otherwise. (Includes Phocion example: counsel may be right even if events go otherwise.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge past decisions by their circumstances at the time
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider what the situation was when you deliberated, not what it is now; the force of all counsel consists in the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reproach yourself for outcomes caused by unforeseen conditions or 'mute' circumstances beyond prudence's reach; blame fortune rather than call it repentance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely chiefly on your own judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Other men’s reasons may fortify your judgments but have little power to dissuade you; use others’ input chiefly to inform, not to replace, your own reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit advice only where you need special information or science; hear others with civility but make use mainly of your own decisions—treat extraneous opinions as flies and atoms that distract the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive regret and vain attempts to alter the past
rubrics_metrics.description: In affairs past, have little regret; imagination and wish cannot move a tittle of what has been fixed in the 'great current of things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief in stoical causes will ease pain about past events; do not let fancy imagine it could reverse past or future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not count infirmity-induced abstinence as true virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Abominate the incidental repentance which old age brings along with it; temperance born of debility is neither chastity nor temperance properly so called.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance ought to be loved for itself and because it is commanded, not because bodily decline makes pleasures impossible; being unable to see pleasure is not resisting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of new vices in old age
rubrics_metrics.description: Old age can bring troublesome maladies of the soul—foolish pride, impertinent prating, superstition, desire of riches, envy, injustice, and malice—more than genuine wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Age imprints wrinkles on the mind; active study and precaution are required to evade or weaken these imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate variety and pliancy of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rivet yourself to one humour or course; the bravest souls have the most variety and pliancy and can apply themselves to divers employments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life is multiform motion; being fixed to one set of inclinations is to be a slave. Adapt and be able to 'stretch and slacken' yourself to different conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer meditation and self-study to merely furnishing the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Meditation is a powerful and full study; fashion your soul rather than merely furnish it with external learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading should rouse reason and employ judgment, not only memory. Books serve to rouse the reason by various objects; the principal use of reading is to exercise judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate desires to attainable goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderate and adapt desires to the nearest and easiest to be acquired things; avoid separating yourself from necessary company or fixedly cleaving to unattainable desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stooping to what is within reach is wise; excessive delicacy of humour deprives one of conveniences of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be adaptable in social conversation across classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Let yourself down to those with whom you converse; be able to discourse with a neighbour about building or hunting and with common followers in their own way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid being pedantic or magisterial in ordinary conversation; adopting natural, unstrained manners prevents alienation and is more equitable between masters and servants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected learnedness and borrowed graces
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not parade pedantic science or 'strew their books everywhere' in common discourse; people of quality should set out their proper natural treasures rather than borrow arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning that cannot penetrate the soul 'hangs still upon the tongue.' If the learned intrude upon ordinary talk, they should humble themselves—learning should be 'suffragan and docile.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Value sincere, private friendship and conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Covet the society of sincere and able men for privacy, frequentation, and conference—the exercise of souls without other fruit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such commerce embraces mature judgment mixed with goodness, gaiety, and friendship; meaningful content can occur in private conferences as much as in public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use books as constant companions and a remedy for idleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Books are more certain and more our own than love or social friendships; they comfort in old age, ease idleness, blunt grievances, and are an unfailing diversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possessing books gives satisfaction even if not constantly read—'I enjoy them as misers do their money'—and they are the best viaticum for life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a private place at home for solitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man should have at home a place to be by himself — to entertain himself alone or conceal himself from others; solitude allows folding oneself within one's skin even in public settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local solitude and a designated study (Montaigne's circular study described) help to sequester oneself from social obligations; ambition makes even great fortunes a form of slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in love with true inclination, not mere pretence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not engage in love without passion (as actors playing parts), nor avoid it entirely out of fear; one must truly desire what one expects to enjoy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty is primary in love; wit is secondary. Dissimulated or mercenary embraces yield little fruit; difficulty and the dignity of lovers can heighten pleasure.
